newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Clark reaffirms will seek no confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Clark reaffirms will seek no confidence vote.

text.p: New Zealand Labour leader Helen Clark reaffirmed on Wednesday that Labour would seek a vote of no confidence in the National government when parliament sits, even faced with an uncontroversial speech from the throne recognising the government's caretaker role.

Labour and caretaker Prime Minister Jim Bolger's conservative National Party are holding separate talks over the shape of the next government with the nationalist New Zealand First Party which holds the balance of power after the October 12 election.
Parliament must meet by December 13. The parties have said they hope to form a government before then.
One of the first acts of the parliament would be the speech from the throne, delivered by the Governor-General but written by the government, which outlines its planned programme.
It is normal for this programme to be rejected by the opposition by way of a no-confidence motion during the debate that follows, known as the address-in-reply debate.
This debate can last for three weeks.
If a new government had not been formed, Clark said she would expect a short and uncontroversial speech recognising the government's caretaker role and its inability to undertake any initiatives.

"That would be the appropriate one. However Mr Bolger may... take the Prebble school of advice which says: Go gungho on a minority government and set out your National Party programme,'" Clark told Reuters.
Free market Act New Zealand Party leader Richard Prebble wants National to call parliament and test its mandate rather than wait for the result of the negotiations with NZ First.
"I would be very surprised if we didn't move a vote of no confidence. You would have to expect others to if we didn't" Clark said, adding the left-wing Alliance and Act were "itching for a debate".
She said even if an address-in-reply motion was moved and a no confidence vote tabled, she expected the government to adjourn the debate.
"We think it is possible the government may not even seek to move and second the address-in-reply debate. We would if they didn't.
"So there will be a debate -- even on the adjournment motion -- which could lapse at the close of the sitting day," Clark said.
She said if a new government was not formed, NZ First was likely to support an adjournment.
"Then we are into February," Clark said. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473 4746
